nameStory: The American emerald gets its name from the metallic green sheen that flashes across its dark body when sunlight hits it just right. Unlike some dragonflies that are boldly colorful, this species earned its 'emerald' title from those subtle but stunning green highlights that shimmer against its mostly black appearance.
description: The American emerald is a medium-sized dragonfly with a sleek, mostly black body that measures about 1.7 to 2.0 inches long. Its dark coloration is broken up by a distinctive bright yellow ring that wraps around where the second and third segments of its abdomen meet. When the light catches it properly, you'll see beautiful metallic green reflections dancing across its body, giving it that emerald quality that inspired its name. This northern dragonfly is built for agile flight and can often be seen patrolling over ponds and slow-moving waters.

idTips.label: Yellow abdominal ring
idTips.description: Look for a bright yellow band wrapped around the abdomen where segments 2 and 3 connect - it stands out like a golden belt against the dark body

idTips.label: Dark body coloration
idTips.description: The body appears almost coal-black in most lighting, feeling smooth and sleek if you could touch it, unlike the rougher texture of some other dragonflies

idTips.label: Metallic green sheen
idTips.description: Turn your head slightly as you watch - the body will flash with brilliant emerald-green highlights when sunlight hits at the right angle

idTips.label: Medium size
idTips.description: About the length of your thumb to the first knuckle of your index finger - noticeably smaller than the giant darners but larger than the dainty pond sprites

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: Wings are transparent like cellophane with dark veins creating a delicate stained-glass pattern, making a soft rustling sound during flight

habitat: American emeralds prefer the edges of clean ponds, slow-moving streams, and marshy areas throughout New England's forests and wetlands. They're often found near waters surrounded by conifers or mixed woodlands, where they can perch on overhanging branches between hunting flights. Look for them at elevations from sea level up into the mountains, especially around beaver ponds and natural forest pools.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, often seen doing their first tentative flights near the water where they developed as aquatic nymphs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time - adults are actively hunting, mating, and laying eggs. This is the best time to spot that distinctive yellow ring and emerald sheen.
seasonality.fall: Adults become less active and eventually disappear as temperatures drop, while eggs and young nymphs remain underwater preparing for next year.
seasonality.winter: No adults visible - they spend winter as aquatic nymphs living under the ice, slowly growing and waiting for spring warmth to trigger their transformation.

funFact: American emerald nymphs are underwater ninjas that can shoot out their extendable jaw like a harpoon to snatch prey - this hinged 'mask' can extend nearly half their body length in milliseconds to grab unsuspecting tadpoles or water bugs.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other dark dragonflies, but that bright yellow abdominal ring is your foolproof field mark - remember 'yellow belt on black body' and you'll never mistake it for anything else in New England.
compareHints: Since this is the only Cordulia species in our dataset for New England, compare it to other emerald dragonflies in the same family. American emeralds are distinguished from their emerald cousins by that unmistakable yellow ring - other emeralds might have metallic green bodies but lack this bold yellow marking. The combination of mostly black coloration with just one bright yellow band makes this species unique among New England's emerald dragonfly family.
